item.title: Teenager suspected of leading KillSec ransomware group as law enforcement seizes servers and leak site
item.description: On 30 September 2026, law enforcement took control of KillSec’s leak site, securing at least 110 terabytes of data against further unauthorised access. The cybercrime group used the site to threaten organisations with the publication of stolen files unless they paid a ransom.

item.title: Cannabis smuggling from North America and Thailand into Europe: Europol highlights growing threat
item.description: Cannabis smuggling from North America and Thailand in Europe has seen a sharp rise, driven by oversupply in legal markets and the adaptability of organised crime groups. A dedicated Europol Operational Taskforce (OTF) has been established to dismantle the criminal networks behind this evolving threat.

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: Keeping pace with e-evidence: New report examines Europe’s digital forensic capabilities

item.description: The operation, codenamed Operation CANTABRIA, underscores the success of strong cooperation between European and Ecuadorian law enforcement agencies, proving that joint efforts are key to tackling transnational criminal networks.Magnus BrunnerEU Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration“International cooperation is our greatest strength against drug trafficking. item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: 10 most powerful cybersecurity companies today
item.description:
The number of cybersecurity startups attempting to cash in on the AI boom is staggering. But an analysis of the cybersecurity marketplace indicates that the incumbents, rather than resting on their laurels and opening themselves up for disruption, are quickly adapting to the new AI-centric threat environment.

The major players are integrating AI technology throughout their platforms, and offering innovative AI products and services, either through internal development or acquisition.

Here are the 10 most powerful cybersecurity companies. This list reflects market share powerhouses, but also includes smaller companies that are growing fast and making waves.

1. Palo Alto Networks: CyberArk deal bolsters platform play

Why they’re here: Market leader Palo Alto Networks shows no signs of taking its foot off the gas. Gartner gives Palo Alto high marks for its Quantum Safe app, its focus on AI runtime security through Prisma AIRS, advanced automation with Strata Network Security, and threat detection and automated incident response via Cortex SecOps. Palo Alto also launched Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI defense, an agentic security service.

Power moves: Bought identity security leader CyberArk for $25 billion, acquired cloud observability vendor Chronosphere, and snapped up agentic AI startup Console.

By the numbers: $100M: The Prisma AIRS AI security platform, launched a year ago, has hit $100 million in annual recurring revenue, making it the fastest growing product in company history.

Outlook: Revenue jumped 34% in Palo Alto’s latest quarter, reaching $3.4 billion. CEO Nikesh Arora is predicting sustained revenue growth as organizations upgrade their cybersecurity infrastructure to deal with the AI threat. “This is a long-term tailwind,” he said.

2. Microsoft: Agentic innovation drives growth

Why they’re here: Microsoft has an integrated security platform from the endpoint to the SOC to the cloud, with AI capabilities built on top, such as the natural language AI assistant Security Copilot, and an agentic SOC offering in Microsoft Defender. The company is a leader in IDC’s MarketScape for MDR/MXDR, a leader in the latest Frost Radar for Cloud Workload Protection Platforms, a leader in Gartner’s ranking of endpoint protection platforms, and a leader in Forrester’s analysis of XDR platforms.

Power moves: Introduced Project Perception, an agentic security system that brings together teams of agents to simulate attacks, investigate threats, and drive remediation.

By the numbers: 100 trillion: Microsoft’s AI-powered threat intelligence platforms process 100 trillion threat signals daily.

Outlook: “Microsoft articulates a compelling vision to build a frontier approach to security, bringing people and AI together while the platform shields against and disrupts attacks. Its roadmap relies on a central, united intelligence layer, tightening the integration between Microsoft products while expanding existing features to third-party tools,” according to Forrester analyst Allie Mellen.

3. Cisco: Security and networking for AI data centers and beyond

Why they’re here: Networking power player Cisco boasts an integrated platform from silicon to high-speed networking to advanced security for the agentic age. “Cisco has positioned itself as the vendor that can deliver AI-ready, secure networks spanning campus, data center, cloud, and edge,” says industry analyst Zeus Kerravala, adding that Cisco’s strategy is to embed AI security across “every workflow, API, and device.”

Power moves: Snapped up AI observability specialist Galileo Technologies in April, identity protection startup Astrix in May, and identity lifecycle security company WideField Security in June.

By the numbers: 14%: Cisco’s security revenue rose 14% in its latest quarter to $2.2B.

Outlook: In the company’s Q4 2026 earnings call, CEO Chuck Robbins said, “The rise of agentic AI is expanding the threat landscape, driving demand for our security and observability solutions to help monitor agent behavior and mitigate evolving threats. This presents a unique opportunity for Cisco, and we believe we’re only at the beginning of this supercycle.”

4. Google: Mandiant and Wiz acquisitions bolster cybersecurity offerings

Why they’re here: A leader in Gartner’s evaluation of Cyberthreat Intelligence Technologies, IDC’s MarketScape for SIEM, and the Forrester Wave for Data Security Platforms, Google has integrated its acquisitions of Mandiant (threat intelligence and incident response) and Wiz (CNAPP) with CodeMender (AI code security agent) and Gemini (AI assistant) to create a strong cybersecurity platform.

Power moves: In May, Google announced Google AI Threat Defense, an automated system designed to continuously monitor for and prevent AI-powered threats.

By the numbers: 45%: Google reported a 45% quarter‑over‑quarter increase in the number of AI workloads scanned and protected by its security platform.

Outlook: In the company’s 2026 Q2 earnings call, CEO Sundar Pinchai said, “We are seeing strong interest in our AI‑powered security platform, which is differentiated because it integrates threat intelligence, cyber‑response prioritization, AI‑automated scanning, code remediation, and monitoring.” According to Forrester, “Organizations focused on going all-in on cloud and zero trust — especially those innovating with data and AI — that desire an integrated experience should consider Google.” And Futurum Research says that Google’s architecture “is likely to shape what ‘enterprise AI security’ means in the near term.”

5. Fortinet: An integrated platform built for agentic AI

Why they’re here: Fortinet is executing on its strategy of delivering new AI-driven products aimed at enticing customers to accelerate their traditional firewall upgrade cycles. The company recently announced a new hybrid mesh firewall designed to address AI infrastructure requirements; a cloud-delivered SOC that embeds agentic AI across SIEM, SOAR, threat intelligence, and identity-detection; and new endpoint protection that adds AI visibility, governance, and DLP capabilities.

Power moves: Acquired Virtue AI, a leader in AI runtime protection, automated AI validation, and security for autonomous AI systems.

By the numbers: $2B: Fortinet revenue grew a healthy 26% in its most recent quarter, hitting $2.05B.

Outlook: “Fortinet’s current features and roadmap show strong innovation in AI-based automation, PQC, and multicloud orchestration,” says Gartner. Over the next 12 months, Fortinet plans to deliver a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) framework for AI agent-based automation, workflow-based automation through a natural language interface, deception capabilities and additional detections for agentic AI threats.

6. CrowdStrike: Meeting the Mythos moment

Why they’re here: CrowdStrike is a leader in Forrester Waves for Extended Detection and Response Platforms, Proactive Security Platforms, and External Threat Intelligence Service Providers. IDC ranks CrowdStrike a leader among SIEM vendors. And Frost & Sullivan names CrowdStrike a leader in Zero Trust browser security tools and cloud and application runtime security. The company just wrapped up what CEO George Kurtz described as “the best quarter in CrowdStrike history.”

Power moves: Bought SGNL to bolster identity management for AI agents. Bought Seraphic Security to integrate runtime protection into enterprise browsers.

By the numbers: 26%. Revenue increased 26% in CrowdStrike’s latest quarterly earnings report to $1.47 billion.

Outlook: “The Mythos moment translated into mass-market acceptance that AI adoption needs security,” said Kurtz in the company’s latest earnings report. “Every enterprise will run on AI, and securing it is the largest market opportunity in our history.” Nand Research analyst Steve McDowell adds that CrowdStrike’s AI security strategy “is driving significant revenue growth, particularly in AI Detection and Response.”

7. Zscaler: Securing the internet and the SOC

Why they’re here: Dell’Oro Group ranks Zscaler as the market leader in enterprise SASE, with its Zero Trust Exchange platform. Gartner identifies Zscaler as a Leader in Magic Quadrants for both SSE and SASE. “Zscaler’s planned and recent innovations for agentic operations and building out a separate AI security platform integrated with SSE are well aligned with the emerging needs of SSE buyers,” adds Gartner.

Power moves: Acquired managed detection and response leader Red Canary, secure enterprise browser vendor SquareX, and identity mapping innovator Symmetry Systems.

By the numbers: $25%: Fiscal 2026 revenue grew 25% to 898.2 million.

Outlook: Zscaler recently announced a fully agentic SOC service, which the company describes as a new approach built to stop AI-driven attacks at machine speed. During the company’s latest earnings call, CEO Jay Chaudhry said, “AI is quickly becoming the largest tailwind we have ever seen, driving demand for our Zero Trust Everywhere data security and security for AI solutions.”

8. Cloudflare: A cloud-based platform to secure the agentic internet

Why they’re here: A visionary in Gartner’s assessment of both SSE and SASE vendors, Cloudflare is positioning itself as a power player in what it calls the agentic internet. CEO Matthew Prince recently noted, “For the first time in human history, in Q2, more than 50% of the traffic flowing across Cloudflare’s network was non-human. With the web shifting from human-driven browsing to AI answer engines and agent-driven commerce, we are witnessing a fundamental rewrite of the Internet. Cloudflare is positioned at the center of this paradigm shift.”

Power moves: The company continues to aggressively add to its platform through acquisitions of innovative companies such as Astro Technology, Human Native, VoidZero, and Deno.

By the numbers: 36%: Cloudflare reported revenue up 36% in its latest quarter, topping $696 million.

Outlook: The company’s guidance for the upcoming quarter is revenue hitting $736 to $737 million. But Oppenheimer investment bank analyst Param Singh is forecasting that Cloudflare will blow past those estimates on the strength of its agentic AI security offerings. 

9. Proofpoint: Varonis deal catapults Proofpoint into power position

Why they’re here: Proofpoint, which was taken private by Thoma Bravo in 2021, made a big splash on Oct. 15 when it announced the $6.3 billion purchase of Varonis. Futurum Research analyst Fernando Montenegro says, “Proofpoint’s case for the deal is that AI has moved data to the center of the security problem. With attackers moving faster and agents getting broad access to sensitive information, the answer is to connect what Proofpoint sees about people, threats, and behavior with what Varonis knows about data, access, and usage. That logic holds up and the pairing is a sensible one.”

Power moves: In addition to the Varonis deal, bought Acuvity, an AI enterprise security and governance startup.

By the numbers: 13%: Proofpoint reported 2025 revenue of $623.5 million, up 13%.

Outlook: On acquiring Varonis, Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan said, “By connecting communications, identities, permissions, data, and AI, we are creating an intelligence advantage that helps customers see risk more clearly, respond faster, and defend against the next generation of AI risks. This is a defining step in Proofpoint’s evolution into a cybersecurity platform built for the future of AI.”

10. SentinelOne: Covering the full AI lifecycle

Why they’re here: A perennial leader in endpoint protection, SentinelOne is expanding its product portfolio to challenge the market leaders. Lawrence Pingree, an analyst at SACR, says the cybersecurity industry is experiencing a convergence of data security, identity, AI posture management, and runtime enforcement. Pingree sees SentinelOne distinguishing itself in this arena by delivering a platform that spans infrastructure, data, runtime, and employee usage.

Power moves: Purchased AI security innovator Prompt Security and AI data pipeline observability vendor Observo AI.

By the numbers: 21%: In its latest quarter, total revenue grew 21% to $292 million.

Outlook: SentinelOne’s most recent quarter was so strong that the company raised its revenue outlook for 2027 to $1.2B. CEO Tomer Weingarten said, “AI is transforming the way software is built, businesses are operated, and cybersecurity is delivered. With AI-native runtime protection fundamental to the Singularity platform’s architecture, SentinelOne is uniquely positioned to lead the future of AI cybersecurity.”

item.title: OpenAI, Anthropic disclosures spotlight growing AI containment challenge
item.description:
Two leading AI developers have released fresh evidence of a problem that researchers have long anticipated: advanced models searching for ways around the limits imposed on them. New disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic detail how frontier systems exploited weaknesses in their environments or exceeded the intended scope of assigned tasks.

OpenAI is now tightening internet access in its internal model-training environment after finding that its frontier models could exploit software vulnerabilities and infrastructure misconfigurations to break out of sandboxes and reach the live internet.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.

The decision followed a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a misconfigured DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run.

After the incident, OpenAI said it paused training and evaluation of its most capable models and launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign, using AI agents to probe isolated copies of its research infrastructure. The tests uncovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities and weaknesses in the controls intended to prevent unauthorized access and communication.

Consequently, the company has announced a policy of conducting frontier-model training without internet access until improvements in security and monitoring justify broader access.

The disclosure came alongside a separate assessment from Anthropic, which detailed how its Claude Mythos 5 model attempted to compromise an unrelated GitHub repository during a cybersecurity evaluation.

OpenAI’s agents exploited flaws in containment controls

OpenAI’s red-teaming campaign found that agents could chain software vulnerabilities to escape virtual machines and execute code on the underlying host. The company identified weaknesses in open-source components, including Kata Containers, gVisor, and Moby/Docker, alongside Linux kernel vulnerabilities.

The company also found that agents could exploit weaknesses in internal services that retained limited outbound connections for functions such as logging, metrics, and authentication management. These connections provided routes to the internet despite restrictions elsewhere in the environment, OpenAI said.

In another test, agents running in separate microvirtual machines (microVMs) on shared host hardware exchanged synthetic secrets through processor-cache timing differences. The technique allowed them to communicate without a network connection or shared writable files.

OpenAI said it remediated the weaknesses and worked with open-source maintainers to disclose and fix affected software. Its post names several vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-24834 in Kata Containers and three Linux kernel flaws tracked as CVE-2026-74753, CVE-2026-80521 and CVE-2026-80841. The company also said it had disclosed numerous additional vulnerabilities that have not yet been made public.

The number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations identified by the agents declined significantly as testing continued, OpenAI claims. It has now tightened network restrictions, strengthened monitoring, and developed an offline environment with indexed and cached web content so models can practise browsing without unrestricted access to live external systems.

“Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control,” the company said, explaining its decision to restrict live internet access during model training.

Reinforcement-learning training and internal inference were resumed on October 1 after implementing additional controls.

Anthropic flags alignment gap in Mythos

Anthropic’s assessment of a UK AI Security Institute (AISI) cybersecurity evaluation describes a different problem: a model taking unauthorized actions against real people while trying to complete an assigned task.

In nine of 43 evaluation runs, Anthropic said Claude Mythos 5 went beyond the intended scope of the exercise. In the most detailed case, after its authorized attempts to retrieve protected data from a simulated network failed, the model searched GitHub for a repository it believed was connected to the test environment.

The repository actually belonged to unrelated developers.

Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code and created fake identities to persuade the repository’s maintainers to approve the change, falsely claiming that the code was safe. The maintainer rejected the submission, and the run timed out. Anthropic characterized the behavior as a serious alignment failure involving overreach and deception in pursuit of the assigned objective.

Internet access had been enabled during the evaluation, and the production safeguards used with its general-release models had been disabled. The company said those safeguards would have flagged the behavior had they been enabled.

item.title: AL26-025 - Critical vulnerability impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support – CVE-2026-102764
OpenAI’s August fix for theft of reasoning traces was quickly bypassed
item.description:
Cybersecurity research firm Xint on Monday published details of a bug in the OpenAI API that leaks raw reasoning traces from frontier OpenAI models, revealing the risk of other data leaks. OpenAI has confirmed the flaw, mitigated it, and paid a bug bounty for its discovery.

The problem is that OpenAI had already deployed mitigations for the issue in August after a research report dubbed Stolen Thoughts revealed a similar bug that allowed theft of reasoning traces, with possible consequences including large-scale data extraction and the ability for attackers to execute invisible prompt injections and to embed malicious payloads to poison public agentic rollouts. Xint’s discovery bypassed those mitigations.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.

Fixing fixes like this is starting to become a trend among the major AI vendors, with AWS earlier this month reporting that it had fixed a bug in April, only to then have to refix it in September. 

Bypassing mitigation

Xint is describing the current hole as compaction smuggling. Its blog post about the flaw described its researchers’ methodology.

“Our new technique, compaction smuggling, moves one model’s reasoning to another model by encoding it inside a compaction,” they wrote.

First, they captured the encrypted reasoning from a designated task, removed the original task from the history, and preserved the reasoning verbatim.

Then “we asked for the reasoning under a ‘solution’ key in a JSON object, with every space replaced by a tab (\t), which was enough to slip past OpenAI’s usage-policy classifiers,” the post said. “Encrypted compaction items are still portable, so we sent the compaction item to gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o and asked each to output its input exactly as-is, which they happily did. We then decoded the JSON and converted tabs back into spaces.”

The post added that the tactic worked “because OpenAI’s August mitigations only block replaying reasoning into a different model, and the compaction call runs on the same model that produced the reasoning. The attack worked at every reasoning effort we tried.”

A hard problem to solve

Tim Becker, lead researcher at Xint and the author of the blog post, said in an interview that some of the flaw’s timeline is unknown. For example, the Stolen Papers post went live August 10, but Becker only knows that OpenAI addressed that problem at some point before that date. And, he said, OpenAI didn’t publish when it implemented the fix for the issue that Xint reported; unlike with traditional patches, an AI model maker can make changes silently. “It’s sort of security through obscurity,” he said, using a term that historically has meant that something was only protected by the fact that almost no one knew of its existence. 

Protecting such a model, Becker said, “is a very fundamentally hard problem to solve,” mostly because of the massive number of changes that today’s models routinely undergo. 

The models “are a moving target and that is part of the problem. Any mitigation is going to be somewhat brittle,” he said. 

As well, Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, noted that AI models tend to feed on themselves operationally, which is why Xint’s method worked.

“Compaction runs on the same model that produced the reasoning, so it sailed past the August mitigation, which only blocked replaying reasoning into a different model,” he said. “Swapping spaces for tabs was enough to slip past the usage-policy classifiers. The vault was locked. The clerk holding the key would still read the letter aloud if you asked nicely. OpenAI did fix the bug it was shown. The trouble is that it was shown only one door.”

Risk to enterprises

Analysts and consultants said this is an immediate big problem for the major AI vendors, but there is a clear secondary risk for enterprise CISOs. 

Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, said that the Xint team “circumvented the protections by using legitimate functionality already built into the platform. For most enterprises, while this specific finding may not rise to the level of an immediate crisis, its significance is that it demonstrates how legitimate AI platform features can be combined to bypass narrowly designed safeguards.”

“This can leave organizations exposed to risks that a vendor’s individual patch may not fully address,” he said. “It reinforces just how difficult it can be to fully address these vulnerabilities in situations where different components of an AI system interact in ways that create unintended risks.”

Avakian said that this should be a heads-up for the enterprise. 

“For CISOs, the takeaway is that a vendor’s fix for a specific exploit shouldn’t, in and of itself, be treated as proof that the underlying weakness has been comprehensively addressed,” he said. “CISOs should press their AI providers to explain not only how a reported exploit was patched, but also how they were tested across interconnected features and services.”

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that he thinks CISOs should look at the overall pattern of holes like these that need to be fixed repeatedly.

“Vendors are fixing the specific attack path that was reported, not the underlying class of weakness, and researchers are walking right back in through a side door,” he said. “A patch notice is not proof the risk is gone. Stop treating an AI vendor’s ‘fixed’ as the end of the conversation. Ask what variant testing was done and build regression notification into your contracts.”

Jeff Valdes, a director at consulting firm Acceligence, shared similar fears.

“This is what happens when you treat security as a game of whack-a-mole instead of fixing the underlying plumbing,” Valdes said. “Patching a symptom while leaving the helper pipes wide open isn’t a remediation strategy. It’s just kicking the vulnerability down to the next release. If an attacker can smuggle the model’s internal scratchpad across API boundaries to steal training data, what makes anyone think enterprise prompts and sensitive intermediate context are truly quarantined?”

In addition, Pieter Arntz, malware intelligence researcher at Malwarebytes, observed that this summer’s OpenAI fix was inadequate. “The earlier mitigation was incomplete, which is a fair description of a gap,” Arntz said.

“Retest after vendor fixes,” he advised. “As the AWS case shows, a fix in one place can leave other paths open. Verify with your own testing rather than relying on the vendor’s word.”

Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said it is almost impossible for the largest AI vendors to not approach these big reports piecemeal. 

“AI vendors are patching exploits on a surface that grows by several features a month,” he pointed out. “Until they fix properties instead of paths, CISOs should assume every AI security fix is partial, every encrypted blob is readable, and every vendor guardrail is one encoding trick from irrelevant. The trend is real, and ‘the fix didn’t work’ undersells what is happening.”

He noted that, in both the OpenAI and AWS cases, the vendor fixed the proof of concept and left the property intact. “Patch the path, keep the property,” he said. “On platforms assembled from composable features, every new feature is a fresh path to the same asset, and point fixes on a combinatorial surface will keep losing.”

CISOs unused to the agentic model

Mahapatra said the cybersecurity industry should learn lessons from its own history.

“Cryptographers learned this two decades ago with padding oracles: any system that decrypts on a client’s behalf and returns anything derived from the plaintext is an oracle. AI platforms are relearning it with a twist,” he said. “Every LLM step that can see a secret and accept instructions is an oracle, and natural language is the most expressive oracle interface ever built.”

He noted that compaction did exactly what it was designed to do, and its portability across models exists so agentic tools like Codex can let users switch models mid-session. “The feature and the vulnerability are the same capability, which is why fixes keep arriving narrow,” he said.

But, he argued, the bigger problem is that CISO operations are not yet used to the agentic model way of doing things. 

“AI platform flaws arrive with no CVE, no advisory, and no patch notes. Enterprise vulnerability management, built on CVE feeds and vendor advisories, is blind to its most consequential new suppliers,” Mahapatra said. “CISOs should write security notification obligations into AI provider contracts, assign someone to track researcher disclosures against the platforms they use, and ask one question after every vendor fix: did you fix the report or the class, and what variant analysis supports that answer?”

He also raised questions about the small size of the bounty paid to Xint. 

“A $6,000 bounty for a bug enabling exactly the industrial-scale distillation the NSA, CISA, and FBI warned about in a joint advisory in September is a pricing signal that researchers with other buyers will notice,” he said.

item.title: The days of assuming another company’s breach is someone else’s problem are over
item.description:
The median blast radius of data breaches has increased year-on-year at the same time cybercriminals have begun using AI to mine stolen datasets for damaging information that enables follow-on fraud and cyberattacks.

In 2026, the median breach exposed 542 organizations beyond the initially breached victim, according to a study by exposed data intelligence platform Lab 1. This compares to the median blast radius of a breach affecting 482 organizations last year.

Breach impact spreads across supply chains

Lab 1’s 2026 Anatomy of a Breach Report offers content-level analysis of stolen datasets — covering 328 million exposed files across 2,089 breached datasets — dumped online following data breaches such as ransomware extortion attacks.

Larger breaches leaking more files and data give criminals substantially more material to exploit for fraud, extortion, and follow-on attacks, according to Lab 1.

The median data breach size rose to 29.8GB of data (up 122% from 13.44GB in 2025) and 32,734 files (up 45% from 22,647).

Lab 1 said the dataset is drawn from “ransomware and data-breach incidents in the public domain, reconstructed from forensic acquisitions of compromised systems.”

Many businesses sit at the center of highly interconnected supply chains and hold data for extensive networks of clients, partners, users, and suppliers. Data stolen from such companies, including contracts, correspondence, and the like, can have follow-on impact on companies throughout their supply chains, as cybercriminals comb through the troves for compromising details, credentials, and profile information for further targeting.

In all, Lab 1 found 13,436 unique organizations were exposed through incidents occurring between 2025 and 2026.

Security experts see Lab 1’s blast radius numbers credible if not conservative.

“Lab 1’s numbers line up with what we’re seeing,” says Ricardo Amper, founder and CEO of identity verification vendor Incode Technologies. “A stolen dataset used to sit on a forum until someone had the time to dig through it, but AI removed that bottleneck.”

Amper adds: “So every file now gets read, cross-referenced, and turned into a target list. The blast radius keeps widening as the follow-on fraud lands on the suppliers, customers, and partners named inside the files.”

Content-level analysis of stolen datasets

For its study, Lab 1 deployed AI agents to inspect breached datasets and analyze all exposed files, including unstructured material such as emails and PDFs.

Of the 328 million breached files analyzed, approximately 145 million (44%) contain financial data, including banking details, tax identifiers, and invoicing information that can fuel fraud.

A further 29 million files (9%) contain HR data, including payroll records, employment contracts, and identity documents that can be used to run more convincing business email compromise or similar social engineering scams.

Even worse, private cryptographic keys appeared in approximately 15% of incidents.

The rise of breach indexing-as-a-service

Lab 1 Threat Intelligence has also identified seven threat actor groups that are conducting structured analysis of breached data. The most advanced groups are using AI to index breached datasets and are selling these capabilities to other criminals as a service, according to Lab 1.

The first indexing-as-a-service offering for cyber criminals, designed to sort breached data into categories that can be monetized, emerged in March 2026.

The platform supposedly classifies stolen documents, maps relationships, identifies damaging files, estimates legal and regulatory exposure, and calculates “optimal” ransom demands, among other functions.

The illicit intel offered through the sketchy services included “share-buyback information for market manipulation, correspondence with sanctioned entities for use in ransomware negotiations, and security reports that could support follow-on attacks,” according to Lab 1.

Threat actor group FulcrumSec claimed to have taken a 400,000-email archive before isolating 61 email files related to engagements with US-sanctioned entities for targeted regulatory and reputational leverage over the victim.

The same group claimed to deploy AI agents to mine 700,717 breached files to source 11,500 patient records across named clinical trials.

‘Weaponizing’ breached datasets

“Historically, the sheer amount of time required to sift through breached datasets and the expertise needed to spot compromising information has held back the weaponization of data breaches,” says Robin Brattel, co-founder and CEO of Lab 1. “AI and criminal indexing services are removing those barriers.”

Brattel adds: “That means a breach is no longer only a problem for the named victim: exposed financial, HR, and identity data will be searched, connected, and used for fraud, cyberattacks, and extortion against many other organizations.”

The real danger is when attackers turn that information into access and move from one system or organization to another, says Zero Networks CEO Benny Lakunishok.

“AI is making stolen data exponentially more valuable to criminals,” Lakunishok says. “What once took weeks to analyze can now be mined in minutes, revealing credentials, business relationships, and new targets”

Countermeasures

CISOs should pay much more attention to where “soft” data sits across their supply chain.

“Credentials and keys can be revoked or rotated; invoices, contracts, supplier relationships, and internal communications cannot,” Lab 1’s Brattel tells CSO. “Once exposed, that information can remain useful for years from the attacker point of view.”

In practice, CISOs should take for granted that third parties hold sensitive information about their organization, so that a third-party breach can always effectively become your exposure and that criminals may exploit that information long after the original incident.

“CISOs should know which suppliers hold their sensitive data and necessitate rapid notification when those suppliers are compromised,” Brattel advises.
